title: A House of Prayer for All Nations
summary: God calls his people to do justice and keep the Sabbath because his salvation is near. He speaks directly to two groups who feared exclusion, foreigners who have joined themselves to the LORD and eunuchs who cannot have children, and promises them a place in his house, a name better than sons and daughters, and acceptance at his altar, for his house will be a house of prayer for all nations. The chapter then turns sharply against Israel's own leaders, blind watchmen and greedy shepherds who care only for their own comfort.
story: Chapter 55 ended the section of comfort addressed to the exiles. Chapter 56 opens the final part of Isaiah (chapters 56 to 66), whose concern is the life of the restored community: how God's people should live while they wait for his salvation to be fully revealed. The first thing it addresses is membership. Who belongs to the people of God? The answer reaches back to the promise that the Servant would be a light to the nations (49:6) and forward to the gathering of all nations in chapter 66. It also sets a pattern for the rest of the book, where the line between the faithful and the faithless runs through Israel itself rather than between Israel and the nations.
historical:
Most scholars place chapters 56 to 66 in the decades after the first return from exile, in the late sixth or early fifth century BC, when a small community in Judah was rebuilding the temple (completed about 516/515 BC) and debating who belonged. Those who hold to Isaiah's authorship of the whole book read these chapters as the prophet addressing a future community (see the introduction). Either way, the questions were live. Exile had scattered Israelites among the nations, and some foreigners had come to worship Israel's God. Some Judean men had served in foreign courts, and Isaiah 39:7 had warned Hezekiah that some of his own descendants would become eunuchs in the palace of Babylon's king.

The books of Ezra and Nehemiah show the same period wrestling with the boundaries of the community, including the separation of foreign wives (Ezra 9 and 10; Nehemiah 13). Scholars differ on how Isaiah 56 relates to those reforms. Some see a direct tension between openness and exclusion; others note that Isaiah welcomes foreigners who have joined themselves to the LORD and keep his covenant, while Ezra and Nehemiah were concerned with marriages that drew Israel into other gods' worship.
cultural:
The law of Deuteronomy 23:1-8 barred a man who had been castrated from the assembly of the LORD, and it excluded certain foreign peoples, such as Ammonites and Moabites, while allowing others after some generations. Eunuchs were common in ancient royal courts, where men were castrated to serve as officials, often against their will. In a culture where a man's name and memory lived on through his sons, a eunuch was a dry tree with no future. God's promise of “a memorial and a name” (verse 5) answers precisely that fear. The Hebrew phrase behind it, yad vashem, is the name of Israel's national memorial to the victims of the Holocaust in Jerusalem, founded in 1953.

The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest, took on special importance during and after the exile. Without temple or land, it was one of the few visible marks that set Israel apart among the nations, and it appears three times in this chapter as the sign of belonging to the covenant. The watchdogs of verse 10 were kept to guard flocks and warn of danger; a mute dog that cannot bark is useless.
literary: The chapter has two sharply contrasting halves. Verses 1 to 8 are a word of promise, framed by the announcement of coming salvation (verse 1) and the gathering of still others (verse 8). At its center stand the direct speeches to the eunuch and the foreigner, each answering their own quoted fear. Verses 9 to 12 are a word of judgment, a mocking invitation to wild beasts to come and devour because the watchmen are asleep. The shepherds' drinking song in verse 12 ends the chapter on their own words, a self-indictment. Many scholars treat verses 9 to 12 as the beginning of a unit that runs into 57:13.

outline.t: Do justice and keep the Sabbath, for salvation is near
The eunuch: a name better than sons and daughters
The foreigner: a house of prayer for all nations

doctrines.note: “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations” (verse 7). God's purpose for his temple was always wider than Israel. Foreigners who love his name and keep his covenant are welcomed as full worshipers, not tolerated outsiders.

The chapter redefines who belongs to God's people: not by birth, physical wholeness, or ancestry, but by joining oneself to the LORD, loving his name, and holding fast to his covenant. It also warns that leaders can be inside the community and still be faithless.

The Sabbath and covenant faithfulness are the marks of belonging here. The law is not set aside; it becomes the way outsiders enter. At the same time, the promise to eunuchs shows God's grace going beyond a specific exclusion in the law of Deuteronomy 23.

words.note: Saris, eunuch, sometimes used more broadly of a court official (Potiphar is called a saris in Genesis 37:36, though he was married). In this chapter the context of having no sons shows the literal sense is meant. The eunuch who calls himself a dry tree hears that he will have a name that will never be cut off.

Nekar, foreignness; with the word for son it means foreigner. These are people of non-Israelite birth who have joined themselves to the LORD. Their fear that God will separate them from his people is answered with a promise of joy in his house and acceptance at his altar.

Tefillah, prayer. The temple is called “My house of prayer,” and a house of prayer for all nations (verse 7). Though the temple was the place of sacrifice, this chapter describes its deepest purpose as a place where all peoples meet God and call on him.

christ: When Jesus drove the merchants out of the temple courts, he quoted verse 7: God's house was to be called a house of prayer for all the nations, but it had been made a den of robbers (Mark 11:17, combining Isaiah 56:7 with Jeremiah 7:11). The trading is generally thought to have taken place in the outer court, the only part of the temple where Gentiles were allowed. In Acts 8 Philip meets an Ethiopian eunuch, a royal official returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading Isaiah 53; Philip baptizes him (Acts 8:27-38). The promise of verses 3 to 5 is fulfilled in him with remarkable precision. Paul's teaching that in Christ Gentiles are no longer strangers but members of God's household (Ephesians 2:19) carries the chapter's vision to its conclusion.

hard.q: Does Isaiah 56 contradict the law in Deuteronomy 23?
hard.a: Deuteronomy 23:1 barred castrated men from the assembly of the LORD, and verses 3 to 8 excluded some foreign peoples. Isaiah 56 welcomes eunuchs and foreigners into God's house. Readers take this in different ways. Some see the prophet announcing a new stage in God's purposes, in which the boundaries of the old covenant are opened up, much as the New Testament describes. Others note that the law already made room for foreigners who joined Israel (Exodus 12:48; Ruth is a Moabite ancestor of David), and that Deuteronomy's exclusions concerned the formal assembly rather than personal faith, so Isaiah is drawing out an openness already present. Critical scholars often see a genuine debate within the postexilic community reflected in different texts. On every reading, the chapter's direction is unmistakable: faithfulness to God's covenant, not ancestry or bodily condition, is what defines his people.

questions: The eunuch calls himself a dry tree. Who in your church or community might feel like that, and what would it look like to give them a name and a place?
Jesus quoted verse 7 when he cleared the temple. What might crowd outsiders out of a place meant to be a house of prayer for all nations today?
The chapter ends with leaders who say tomorrow will be like today, only better. How does comfort make people blind to what God is doing?
